entries.content:
Dr. Lukas Fieber

Co-Founder & CTO, lemonflow

Konstantin Huneke

Co-Founder & CEO, lemonflow

Welcome back to The Blueprint, a regular feature where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies. We hope to inspire others looking to innovate in their work.

As the electric vehicle revolution gains steam in Europe, every charging session is a moment of truth, for the driver and for the transition itself. At lemonflow, we build AI agents purpose-built for EV charging: support agents for drivers and monitoring agents for charging networks. Our support agents answer drivers around the clock in more than 90 languages, and today they help an EV driver every 90 seconds. 

The Challenge

Before we founded lemonflow, we worked closely with leading mobility players across Europe and saw first-hand how often charging goes wrong: Between 15% and 25% of EV charging attempts in Europe end in failure. Across Europe’s rapidly expanding EV market, where battery-electric car sales grew 30% in 2025 and thousands of charge point operators run public chargers, drivers who encountered stalled charging points were often left stranded or stuck in slow call center queues.

We set out to change that hands-on: to bring the cutting edge of AI to EV charging, and to build the world’s best conversational AI for distributed hardware, an automated platform that resolves real-time charging issues via phone, chat, email, and WhatsApp. However, handling live voice support created several technical requirements:

  • Strict latency thresholds: Frustrated drivers want immediate assistance. Our testing confirmed that serving latencies above 800 milliseconds risk conversational barge-ins, causing drivers to interrupt the agent and break the interaction flow.
  • Managed API bottlenecks: Initially relying on managed LLM APIs, we faced latency deviations during peak hours (spiking from 1.0–1.2 seconds to over 1.7 seconds) and experienced HTTP 429 rate-limit errors when global usage peaked.
  • Compute-intensive conversations: Every agent works from one comprehensive prompt, paired with dynamic tool calls that read and act on live charger data. This design creates intense bursts of compute demand during calls, making throughput on shared, managed capacity difficult to guarantee under peak loads.
  • Highly fragmented ecosystem: We needed a standardized conversational engine capable of bridging around 30 distinct Charge Point Management Systems (CPMS), the backends operators use to run their chargers, each with its own APIs, data models and quirks.
  • Hundreds of tailored agents: No two operators run support the same way. Each has its own tariffs, payment methods, escalation paths and hours for human backup, and most run several agents, for example one per country, brand or hotline, with behavior that can change by time of day. Each agent’s prompt is unique and must be served at full speed and improved without breaking any of the others.

To deliver ultra-low-latency voice interactions and guaranteed serving capacity, we needed direct control over our model hosting environment.

The Solution

We wanted every driver to get best-in-class support that feels effortless, almost magical: no queue, no menu, just a short conversation that ends with the car charging. Picture a driver on a long cross-border trip, pulling into a motorway service station at 11 p.m. She plugs in, but the charger won’t start: the previous session never closed properly. She calls the number on the charger and is answered in her own language. Within seconds, our agent spots the stuck session in the charger’s logs, restarts the charger remotely and stays on the line until power is flowing.

To get there, we had to solve our latency bottlenecks and secure dedicated compute capacity. We migrated from managed APIs to self-hosting the open Gemma 4 model on Google Cloud TPU v6e hardware in the EU.

Like many startups using Gemma, the compatibility of these open models with Gemini allowed us to transition our existing prompt infrastructure with minimal modification.

Moving to self-hosted TPUs unlocked the more complete architectural control our engineering team required to establish a deterministic core layer that handles EV-specific guardrails, guards against prompt injections, and standardizes previously fragmented backend protocols into our internal format before ever reaching the LLM. Control had a second payoff: because the model and serving stack change only when we change them, every test result stays meaningful. That stability laid the foundation for Agent Coach, our background coaching engine for AI agents, described below.

We then developed an intelligent routing gateway to prioritize workloads according to operational urgency, serving live voice calls first, followed by web chats, and deferring automated re-simulations to low-traffic periods.

Custom optimizations to the open-source vLLM serving engine and memory tiering between the TPU and host memory let a single TPU slice keep many more operator agents ready for instant answers, without recalculating their context.

We also implemented automated fallback routing to self-hosted GPUs and Gemini Enterprise endpoints. Thanks to TPU reliability, Gemma answers more than 99.9% of all live conversation turns, and these fallbacks serve primarily as deployment buffers during system updates. Primary or fallback, every request is served from secure EU compute.

The Architecture

The Outcome

For the e-mobility companies we work with, and for their drivers, the result is support that simply works: our agents typically answer every call, handle more than 80% of conversations end to end without a human handover, and earn 95% driver satisfaction. Behind the scenes, self-hosting Gemma on Google Cloud TPUs transformed our performance:

  • Rapid deployment cycles: Prompt update and test cycle times dropped from 2–3 hours to about 10 minutes, a more than tenfold faster improvement loop.
  • Sub-second serving latency: We lowered our P50 latency to around 350 milliseconds and our P90 latency to around 600 milliseconds. That is roughly three times faster than our managed-API baseline and fast enough to sharply reduce customer barge-ins.
  • Zero throttling and flat latency: Dedicated TPU infrastructure eliminated HTTP 429 rate-limit errors, and latency stays flat through peak afternoon call traffic.
  • Testing without limits: On dedicated capacity, every TPU cycle that live conversations don’t need becomes testing capacity, so our team can experiment and validate at will.
  • Built for scale: Today, our agents support more than 40 charging networks in 17 countries, covering more than 250,000 charge points, around the clock. And this is just the beginning: the same platform is ready to take on many more networks and markets.

With additional compute capacity, we introduced Agent Coach, a background engine that provides agents with relevant context during live calls and turns real conversations into permanent test cases, so every call makes the next one better. We also added nightly automated regression testing across thousands of fixed conversational scenarios.

Looking ahead, we are preparing to move to Ironwood, Google’s seventh-generation TPU, as soon as it is available in our EU region. With six times the high-bandwidth memory per chip, Ironwood will multiply the number of operator agents a single TPU can keep ready in memory for instant answers.

Ultimately, our goal is that no driver is ever left stranded at a charger. They get an instant, expert answer in their own language, the charger is rebooted remotely if necessary, and our AI monitoring agents catch the next fault before another driver ever notices. Open models on dedicated Cloud TPUs give us the speed and control to make that the standard across Europe.

The Details

Our platform runs two kinds of AI agents: support agents that talk to drivers in real time, served by Gemma on Cloud TPUs for minimal latency, and monitoring agents that analyze conversations and charger logs in the background on Gemini, so operators can fix faults before the next driver is affected. To keep its core platform consistent across many kinds of e-mobility companies, from charge point operators (CPOs) and e-mobility service providers (eMSPs) to charger manufacturers, lemonflow built a translation layer that converts varied CPMS interfaces into a standardized format.

When a driver calls the support line posted on a charger, the call reaches our Conversational Engine through the operator’s own hotline. The engine then pulls the charger’s live status and Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP) logs, the messages chargers exchange with their backend, from the operator’s CPMS in real time. Because charging stations often lack digital displays, drivers are frequently unaware of underlying issues like pending mobile 3D-Secure payment authorizations, session timeouts, charging cards not enabled for roaming, power reduced by local load management, or a car that ended the session at its own charge limit. Our engine feeds structured log summaries directly into Gemma on TPU to inform interactions with drivers.

Direct model control allows us to stream token output selectively. Partial text tokens stream instantly to our Text-to-Speech (TTS) engine, while structured tool-call tokens stream asynchronously to backend systems to execute real-world actions, such as remotely restarting chargers, unlocking stuck cables, stopping sessions that failed to end, sending drivers details via SMS or email, or notifying service technicians.

Deterministic security controls screen inputs before they reach the TPU-hosted LLM, blocking malicious prompts. This architecture is designed with European critical-infrastructure requirements in mind, and it still keeps conversations snappy, with a typical response starting in around 350 milliseconds.

In the end, all of this should stay invisible to the driver: they just get a fast answer and a charger that works. We’re proud to work with Google Cloud to make that the norm and help EV adoption keep growing.

entries.content:
Paul Ramsey

Product Manager, AI for AlloyDB & Cloud SQL

Transactional databases store vast amounts of unstructured text — clinical notes, customer reviews, support tickets, invoices, and property descriptions. Historically, working with this text meant building complex application code: You had to export data from the database, call external model endpoints, write custom prompt wrappers, parse unpredictable responses, manage retry logic, and update database records. This application-side loop creates operational friction. It introduces query latency, bloats application code, increases model token costs, and creates data compliance risks by moving sensitive information across multiple network boundaries.

We built AlloyDB AI to bring Gemini world knowledge directly into your operational database. Rather than treating artificial intelligence as a disconnected external service, we integrated model intelligence directly into the database engine. Today, we are announcing the preview of two new SQL functions in the AlloyDB AI query engine — 

ai.classify
and 
ai.extract
— available in the 
google_ml_integration
extension (version 1.6.1 or later) on PostgreSQL 18, allowing you to perform classification and structured extraction directly inside your database using standard SQL. Supported by smart batching for AI functions (previously known as AI Function Acceleration), these functions deliver production scalability and performance. 

Now, let’s take a look at these new functions and how to use them.

Classifying text directly in SQL with ai.classify

The 

ai.classify
function categorizes text into user-defined classes without requiring manual prompt engineering. You can specify categories as a simple list of labels or provide a list containing label names and descriptions to guide model context.

Key capabilities include:

  • Single-label classification (

    output_mode => 'single'
    ) to assign the single best category

  • Multi-label classification (

    output_mode => 'multi'
    ) to return all matching categories

  • Category descriptions using 2D arrays to provide explicit context for each label

  • Few-shot prompting by supplying inline examples

  • Flexible execution modes for individual rows (

    TEXT
    ), arrays (
    TEXT[]
    ), and cursors (
    REFCURSOR
    )

Here’s a quick example showing how you can classify customer feedback directly within a SQL query:

Extracting structured JSON with ai.extract

The 

ai.extract
function transforms unstructured text into structured JSON data matching your target schema — specified as a JSON schema or a text list of fields. It handles system instructions internally, saving you from writing prompt templates or response parsers.

Key capabilities include:

  • Schema flexibility supporting standard JSON schemas or plain text field lists

  • Automatic transformation of unstructured text into machine-readable JSON

  • Overloaded function signatures for single rows, arrays, and cursor batching

Here’s an example extracting clinical fields from free-form medical notes:

Speeding up queries with smart batching

Running AI evaluations row-by-row can slow down query execution. AlloyDB addresses this with smart batching for AI functions. When you use 

ai.classify
or 
ai.extract
in SQL 
WHERE
clause expressions, the database engine automatically groups inputs into optimized micro-batches before sending them to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform models.

Smart batching delivers significant performance and efficiency improvements:

  • Faster inference for query execution compared to row-at-a-time evaluations

  • Reduces total model token spend by optimizing input prompt overhead

Real-world industry applications

Native classification and extraction functions support operational workflows across key industry sectors:

  • Healthcare: Securely convert free-text clinical notes into structured records containing patient names, symptoms, and prescribed medications, keeping patient data safely within the confines of the database.

  • Financial services: Extract vendor details, invoice dates, and line-item totals from scanned document text.

  • Legal technology: Pull governing law, liability caps, and termination notice periods from contract documents.

  • Real estate: Extract property types, bedroom counts, and price ranges from descriptive listing text.

  • Knowledge graphs: Extract entities and relationships from documents to populate PostgreSQL Property Graph (PGQ) structures.

Next steps and getting started

We are continuing to expand in-database AI capabilities in AlloyDB, with upcoming enhancements planned for advanced cost optimization, line-level provenance tracking, and query pushdowns beyond 

WHERE
clauses.

To start using 

ai.classify
and 
ai.extract
in your database:

  • Review the AlloyDB AI Query Engine documentation.

  • Explore the AlloyDB release notes.

entries.content:
Gary Eimerman

Managing Director, Google Cloud Learning

Ravi Rajamani

VP, Applied AI & FDEs

It just got easier to prove your expertise in building production-ready agents. Today, Google Cloud is introducing the Professional Agentic Architect certification as the latest milestone in our Gemini Agent Ready (GEAR) initiative. Nearly one million developers are using GEAR to skill up on agents, but what makes this particular certification so special is its adoption within Google’s walls.

Over the past four months, Google Cloud has trained thousands of forward deployed engineers and strategic partners on our own advanced curriculum. Originally built as an internal training initiative, we are now opening it up to the entire developer community and partner ecosystem through this new certification.

As the VP who manages our forward-deployed engineers here at Google Cloud (Ravi) and the managing director of Google Cloud learning (Gary), we’ve seen just how effective this program has been inside Google at helping our teams rethink the way they build, deploy, and use AI in everyday in almost every way. We’re equally about what this new certification can bring to everyone — developers, engineers, and anyone else ready to demonstrate their agentic leadership.

A new hybrid format to validate your real-world skills

This is not a traditional multiple choice exam. Google has introduced a new hybrid format that requires you to prove both conceptual know-how and hands-on execution.

  • Part 1 (The multiple choice proctored exam): Evaluates your system design choices, architectural standards, cost optimization, and security governance.

  • Part 2 (Hands-on labs on Google Skills): Puts you in an active cloud environment to build, test, and debug live agentic workflows.

Why earning this certification can help advance your career

As enterprises look to find top AI talent, this certification immediately signals that you have the advanced skills necessary to design secure, governed, and high-performance multi-agent systems.

Our research with Ipsos on AI skill building shows that certifications drive more recruiter outreach: 82% of learners using Google Skills say that mentioning Google Cloud certifications on their resume drives more recruiter responses.

And it’s not just about getting the call — it’s about being able to answer it. That same research showed that 90% of cloud professionals say credentials like Google Cloud certifications give them the verified know-how needed to fill in-demand roles.

What’s covered on the exam

The certification validates your proficiency across five key domains:

  • Build agents using low-code tools (democratizing rapid agent prototyping).

  • Use coding agents for application development (supercharging your coding productivity).

  • Develop custom agents on the Gemini platform with open source frameworks.

  • Evaluate and deploy agentic workflows (monitoring, optimizing, and ensuring performance).

  • Secure and govern agentic workflows (protecting sensitive enterprise data and ensuring model safety).

Battle-tested by thousands of Google Cloud engineers and partners — now available to you

Enterprise demand for agentic workloads has skyrocketed. As our customers move past AI prompting and run their most business critical workloads on Google Cloud, we’ve built our own team that delivers the agentic future with them — at scale. Google Cloud partners and Google’s forward deployed engineers are embedded directly with customers around the world and are prepared to solve deep technical challenges because of this rigorous curriculum and certification.

While building our forward-deployed engineering program, we wanted to standardize training and upskilling for customers, Google Cloud partners, and our own engineers with the Professional Agentic Architect certification. This ensures our own teams are using the same world-class standards that we recommend to our customers and partners, allowing us to learn from each other and sharpen our skills together.

Skill up for your certification at no cost today

  • Register for Gemini Agent Ready to get access to 35 free monthly learning credits on Google Skills. For Google Cloud customers, Get Certified provides a cohort-based, guided certification journey at no cost. 

  • For Google Cloud partners, register for Partner Certification Kickstart and review the partner learning path.

  • Review the exam guide, learning path and sample questions.

  • Get hands-on with Google Skills labs and preparation modules to get comfortable developing custom agents on Gemini platform with open source frameworks.

  • Register for the multiple-choice exam, complete the hands-on lab requirements, and claim your digital badge to showcase your expertise to the world.

Don't just prompt AI — architect it. Get certified today.

entries.content:
Noel Kenehan

Head of Gemini factory

Renee Li

Technical Solutions Consultant

With the new unified Gemini experience, enterprises can bring third-party partner capabilities directly in Gemini through standardized connectors (spanning Model Context Protocol (MCP), Agent-to-Agent (A2A) runtimes, and REST APIs), alongside emerging declarative skills and plugins.

For independent software vendors (ISVs), this unified architecture unlocks a powerful opportunity to embed domain-specialized intelligence, regulated workflows, and live systems of record directly into enterprises' daily workflows. Yet turning a compelling use case into an enterprise-ready integration often stalls in engineering friction, from choosing the right extensibility primitive and wiring authentication to orchestrating multi-step tool execution and rendering inline interactive experiences.

To eliminate these bottlenecks, Google Cloud launched the Gemini factory—an intensive co-innovation initiative designed to help enterprise software partners go from a blank whiteboard to agentic solutions listed on Google Cloud Marketplace in record time. Through hands-on workshops in global technology hubs—including San Francisco, New York City, Sunnyvale, London, Paris, Tel Aviv, and Tokyo—Google Cloud specialists work side-by-side with partner teams to ideate, architect, and build the next generation of enterprise AI solutions with Gemini.

Specifically, the Gemini factory helps partners:

  • Choose the right agentic architecture across MCP connectors, skills, plugins, and autonomous agents.

  • Go from an initial use case to a production integration in days rather than months.

  • Accelerate customer activation with funding incentives and go-to-market (GTM) support.

Let’s dive in and see how we make all of that a reality.

Choosing the right architecture: agents, MCPs, skills, and plugins

In previous iterations of enterprise AI, third-party integrations often operated as isolated top-level agents, forcing employees to leave their workflow. When software providers arrive at the Gemini factory, they evaluate how their capabilities plug into Gemini across four complementary architectural primitives rather than competing extremes:

  • Model Context Protocol (MCP) connectors: The foundational data and tool pipe for exposing external APIs, search, and CRUD operations to Gemini as callable tools registered in Agent Registry in Gemini platform.

  • Declarative Skills (.md): Open Markdown configurations stored in Skills Registry that equip Gemini with domain-specific instructions, operational guardrails, and repeatable multi-step workflows across connectors.

  • Plugins: The composite packaging and governance primitive in Gemini and Google Cloud Marketplace that bundles one or more Connectors and Skills into a single turnkey solution for IT administrators to govern and Gemini users to invoke.

  • AI agents (A2A): For enterprise ISVs whose value lies in proprietary algorithms, regulated workflows, or strict compliance rules, standalone A2A agents run in an isolated partner environment while plugging into Gemini as callable connectors—keeping intellectual property protected, guaranteeing deterministic execution sequences, and maintaining tamper-proof audit trails.

Rather than forcing developers into a single mold, Gemini unifies all four primitives into a coherent enterprise fabric—passing shared session context into partner connectors and chaining outputs across the enterprise ecosystem.

Technical velocity: From use case to production

Once the right architectural pattern is defined, the Gemini factory compresses months of integration work into a streamlined, AI-assisted engineering pipeline that brings partner development teams and Google Cloud experts together side-by-side.

Accelerated Partner Development Pipeline

This execution velocity is powered by three core capabilities in Gemini platform:

  • Antigravity & AI-assisted builder workflows: Rather than writing boilerplate from scratch, developers build and govern solutions in Antigravity, an AI-first development environment. Using pre-built Rapid Agent Development (RAD) skills and AI-assisted workflows, partner teams rapidly translate use-case specifications into working architectures, scaffold remote MCP connectors or agent runtimes, author declarative 

    .md
    skills, and run automated pre-ingestion validation harnesses.

  • Flexible backend primitives (MCP, skills, plugins, and ADK): For most integrations, teams expose platform APIs via a hosting-agnostic Remote MCP Connector (on Cloud Run or their existing cloud) and layer on declarative Skills (.md) bundled into a turnkey Plugin. When a use case requires closed-IP models or strict deterministic execution, partners use the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) and the A2A protocol to expose their runtime as a callable connector in Agent Registry.

  • Inline adaptive experiences (native MCP apps): Instead of redirecting users to fragmented external portals or maintaining complex custom UIs, Gemini keeps users in the flow of work. Through native MCP apps and guided inline components, partner integrations dynamically stream rich, context-aware visual canvases directly in Gemini while chaining outputs across Google Workspace and other enterprise connectors.

From working prototype to marketplace distribution

The Gemini factory is structured as an end-to-end commercial runway, not just a hackathon:

  • Enterprise deployment architecture: Regardless of whether a partner builds a Skill, Plugin, MCP server, or A2A agent, the architecture is designed to keep customer onboarding frictionless and partner IP secure. Gemini users access the partner integration in Gemini using native OAuth, Dynamic Client Registration (DCR), and streamlined Bring Your Own License (BYOL) flows, while the partner maintains backend security, data sources, and proprietary tooling within their own project perimeter.

  • Built-in discoverability: Partner solutions are published directly to Google Cloud Marketplace and featured in AI Solution Finder, giving enterprise customers a central place to discover validated MCP connectors, plugins, and agents today—and making it simple for IT administrators to configure and govern them in Gemini.

  • Comprehensive incentives & go-to-market: Google Cloud supports verified partners through every growth stage. Qualified solutions unlock Seed Credits upon Marketplace publishing and performance credits to offset operational inference costs, paired with GTM assets and sales enablement to turn engineering milestones into a net-new pipeline.

Featured partners: proven speed to impact

Recent Gemini factory (previously referred to as the Agent Factory) cohorts have already brought a wave of industry-specific agents to life. Here is how nine software partners took complex enterprise challenges and deployed production-grade solutions built with Gemini in days:

Aily Labs

Aily Decision Intelligence Agent

The Aily Decision Intelligence Agent unifies 360° enterprise performance metrics to deliver predictive business diagnostics and actionable strategic recommendations. Built for executive decision-makers, it interrogates complex operational and financial datasets to forecast performance trends, identify supply disruptions, and guide strategic resource allocation through an intuitive, mobile-first interface.

“Our mission is to bring real-time, AI-powered decision intelligence to every business executive. The Agent Factory workshop was an incredible catalyst; it enabled our team to wire up complex predictive reasoning models into the Gemini Enterprise runtime, activating Aily Super Agent in record time; orchestrating thousands of specialized agents, connecting insights across multiple business domains, and presenting them through a single, intuitive interface for the user. Having side-by-side engineering support helped us prove out high-impact executive scenarios and accelerate our roadmap toward a verified listing on Google Cloud Marketplace.”

— Reynaldo Espana, VP of Engineering, Aily Labs

FlowX

Capital Markets Document Reconciliation Agent

FlowX's Capital Markets Document Reconciliation Agent streamlines high-stakes financial operations, including institutional document extraction, multi-party reconciliation, and loan pack completeness audits. Leveraging specialized document intelligence and Kubernetes-backed agent runtimes, it cross-checks disparate contracts, regulatory filings, and credit documentation to flag discrepancies in real time, drastically reducing cycle times for back-office operations.

“In capital markets and lending, precision, auditability, and data security are non-negotiable. What impressed us most about the Agent Factory was how rapidly we could implement complex business validation rules and multi-source document ingestion without compromising on enterprise compliance. Transitioning from raw use cases to a functional prototype in a single workshop demonstrated the sheer execution velocity possible on Gemini.”

— Serban Chiricescu, Founder & Chief Technology Officer, FlowX.AI

Klarvant

Digital Governance Analyst Agent

The Analyst Agent by Klarvant provides outside-in discovery and analysis of an enterprise’s external namespace: post-quantum readiness, certificate and TLS hygiene, email security, supply-chain risk, and external exposure. It tracks post-quantum migration endpoint by endpoint, matches supplier and dependency events to the points where they touch the estate, and answers plain-language questions with audit-ready evidence and custom dashboards built on request.

“What Gemini does exceptionally well is reason over complex technical evidence and explain it in plain language. That is exactly what governance needs. A board member or even a CISO does not want a list of ciphers; they want to know whether the company is ready and what to do next. With the Agent Factory, Gemini became the bridge between our intelligence and the people accountable for it.”

— Endre Fehn, Chief Technology Officer, Klarvant

NextLM

AI Prospecting Agent

The NextLM AI Prospecting Agent brings tenant-native prospect intelligence into Gemini. Powered by the Savant model family, it ranks the B2B accounts and buyers most likely to convert using behavioral data across 300M+ companies, 370M+ professionals, and 1.3B+ tracked news articles. Each customer gets an isolated model that is further trained on its own closed-won and closed-lost data, so prioritization reflects what actually wins for that business. Built to work alongside other agents in Gemini, it hands ranked accounts and buyer context to research, outreach, and CRM connectors, turning “who should we pursue and why now” into action across the workflow.

“Building autonomous B2B sales agents requires blending live external market signals with deep enterprise CRM context. The Agent Factory eliminated the typical development friction—our engineers used the RAD framework to go from an initial architecture diagram to an active, working prospecting agent in under 24 hours. The hands-on co-engineering with Google Cloud gave us the confidence and tooling to bring a production-ready solution straight into the Gemini Enterprise ecosystem.”

— Chris Anzalone, Founder & CEO, NextLM

Optimizely

Mark Marketing Calendar Deck Builder Agent

Optimizely Mark Marketing Calendar Deck Builder Agent converts cross-functional marketing strategies, campaign timelines, and experimentation roadmaps into executive-ready slide decks and visual briefs. Grounded in campaign performance metrics and content repository data, it enables marketing leaders to generate unified omnichannel schedules, align global teams, and track milestone delivery in seconds.

“Marketing teams spend countless hours manually consolidating disjointed campaign plans and roadmaps into presentations for leadership. The Agent Factory allowed us to harness Gemini and Vertex AI Vector Search to turn that manual chore into an autonomous, one-click experience. In just one intensive day, our team built an agent that unlocks immediate productivity gains for enterprise marketers and seamlessly plugs into our broader Mark platform.”

— Kevin Li, SVP Product, Optimizely

Ping Identity

PingID Device Management Agent

Employees manage their own MFA devices just by asking. When someone gets a new phone, the agent displays a live PingID pairing QR code with real-time status directly in Gemini, rendered with A2UI. Employees can also list, rename, set a default, or remove devices without opening a portal or filing a help desk ticket. That replaces a help desk call, and the over-the-phone identity check that social engineering attacks exploit, with a short conversation.

“Every new phone and every last day at work is an identity event, and too many of them still turn into help desk tickets. Working side by side with Google Cloud in the Agent Factory, we built agents that let employees manage their own MFA devices and let admins resolve identity requests in one conversation. With ADK, A2A, and A2UI, those experiences run natively in Gemini, and every action stays scoped to the user, confirmed by a person, and accountable.”

— Loren Russon, SVP, Product & Technology, Ping Identity

Sinch

Sinch RCS Messaging Agent

The Sinch RCS Messaging Agent enables enterprises to create and manage RCS business agents, draft interactive messaging campaigns directly from natural-language prompts, execute rich RCS broadcasts, and monitor delivery reports, built with Gemini and Sinch's carrier infrastructure.

“Collaborating with the Agent Factory team dramatically accelerated our timeline from prototype to a verified listing on Google Cloud Marketplace. Leveraging their structured environment and pre-built RAD skills, our engineering team was able to rapidly assemble, secure, and validate a complete lifecycle agent for RCS, covering enterprise authentication, RCS agent provisioning, prompt-based campaign drafting, and real-time delivery reporting. We walked away with a production-ready solution that harnesses Google Cloud’s ecosystem to help businesses deliver richer, more interactive conversational experiences at scale.”

— Antoine Sein, Senior Engineering Manager, Developer Experience & Agent Experience, Sinch

THG Ingenuity

Shopping Assistant Insights Agent

Shopping Assistant Insights converts shopper conversations into actionable commercial insights and plain-business answers grounded in BigQuery analytics. It tracks shopper demand, assistant performance, and customer friction while maintaining strict data privacy. Designed for commercial leaders, it highlights opportunities to stock, promote, or fix based on real user interactions.

“Our AI Shopping Assistant captures a depth of shopper intent that traditional search bars can't. The Agent Factory helped us turn this insight into valuable action points for brands and retailers. We leveraged Gemini to rapidly build a Shopping Insights Agent that turns raw consumer data into actionable business strategy. The collaborative environment accelerated our development, giving us a deeper understanding of the Agent Marketplace while delivering a live, functional agent that provides immediate value to our customers.”

— Jo Drake, CTO, THG Ingenuity

Xiatech

Xfuze Order Intake Agent

The Xfuze Order Intake Agent automates multichannel commerce order processing, exception triage, and inventory reconciliation across disparate enterprise systems. Powered by Xiatech’s Xfuze integration platform and BigQuery analytics, it continuously identifies supply chain anomalies, resolves fulfillment errors, and provides commercial operators with conversational visibility into real-time order-to-cash health.

“Connecting disparate legacy systems, e-commerce storefronts, and ERPs is a major hurdle for retail and supply chain leaders. At the Agent Factory, we leveraged the Antigravity IDE and RAD developer skills to build an agent that unifies these complex data streams effortlessly. The speed of execution was remarkable, in 24 hours, we built a first of its kind agentic application (multiple agents in one) that delivers instant operational transparency and tangible cost savings to our clients.”

— Jonathan Summerfield, Founder & Chief Executive Officer, Xiatech

The road ahead

The transition to the agentic era requires more than standalone applications—it demands an open, interoperable enterprise ecosystem. Through the Gemini factory, Google Cloud is bringing together technical velocity and commercial scale so partners can meet enterprises wherever they work:

  • End-to-end co-engineering: Rapid architecture design, AI-assisted development, and automated readiness testing in Antigravity alongside Google Cloud partner engineers.

By collapsing the journey from initial whiteboard concept to a verified Google Cloud Marketplace listing into a matter of days, the Gemini factory is helping partners bring the next generation of enterprise AI solutions to market faster than ever—and this is just the beginning. entries.content:
Manish Gaur

Cloud & AI Security Architect

Collin Frierson

Cloud & AI Security Architect

As many developers use agentic tools to create more code faster than ever before, the code has gotten more complex and they’re taking longer to find and fix software flaws.

Helping to address that pressure is a key concern at Google. We know that software development velocity is increasing, as much as 2x for some teams, and the average developer fix time for software flaws expanded from approximately 59 days a decade ago to more than 170 days in 2025, according to the Mandiant M-Trends 2026 Report.

To help you secure more code, more quickly, we’ve built CodeMender, our autonomous code-security agent that can find and fix software flaws at machine speed.

We also know that developer tools only succeed if they fit into existing routines. That’s why CodeMender, part of our AI Threat Defense platform, brings automated code fixes directly into the developer workflow. Today, we’re sharing this reference architecture that wires automated CodeMender remediation straight into Git pull requests via Google Cloud Run.

What the developer sees

Everything happens in the timeline. The scan posts one comment, a table of findings, each finding with an ID, and the two things you can type next.

Figure 1: A pull request triggers the scan on Cloud Run. Findings, exploit traces, and proposed patches all come back to the same timeline.

Reply 

/verify 612424da
and the exploit attempt comes back in the thread, folded into a collapsible View Exploit Steps & Response Trace block so it doesn't bury the conversation.

Reply 

/fix 612424da
and the patch arrives the same way, behind Preview Proposed Code Diff, with a draft pull request already open 
/approve
there. Both commands take 
all
in place of an ID.

Figure 2: The initial scan comment provides a table of findings and the actionable slash commands, keeping the developer entirely within the pull request timeline.

Nothing asks the developer to leave the pull request or learn a console.

Ship evidence, not just a severity

CodeMender 

cm find
runs return a confidence score on the vulnerability finding during the code analysis. If the confidence score is below 100%, you can use 
cm verify
to have CodeMender build and simulate an exploit in a sandbox to determine if the vulnerability is actually exploitable.  

The simulation results can change the severity. Because the verification sandbox is ephemeral, the pipeline automatically streams these artifacts to Google Cloud Storage to preserve an audit trail for compliance and security operations reviews.

Figure 3: The /verify command returns a trace of the sandboxed exploit attempt, giving reviewers actionable evidence rather than abstract alerts.

Engineer for failure modes in your verification pipeline. If your harness only searches for a successful exploit string, then any test failure — such as a crashed mock server or an execution timeout — can cause the pipeline to fail open and mistakenly label a real vulnerability as safe.

Ensure your parser separates true negative results from test crashes. If an exploit fails to complete cleanly, flag the status as inconclusive rather than giving it a clean bill of health.

Propose the patch, preview the diff

When an exploit proves a finding is real, the next step isn't a ticket, it's a patch: 

cm fix a1b2c3d4
instructs CodeMender to author one.

Figure 4: The /fix command returns a unified code diff, giving reviewers meaningful context to evaluate the patch.

If the diff looks good, applying it takes one step. The developer replies 

/approve
. The agent commits the patch to the branch, pushes it, and sets a commit status 
security/codemender-gate
to green. Branch protection is what turns that status into a merge block; without it, the gate is advisory.

No stored keys between GitHub and Cloud Run

None of this happens until GitHub and Google Cloud trust each other. This agent needs write access to your source code, precisely the credential you don't want sitting in a secret store waiting to leak. GitHub Actions can mint a short-lived OIDC token instead, and Google can be configured to accept it, so nothing long-lived exists to steal.

Nearly all the security here rests on one line:

Every GitHub Actions workflow shares that issuer URL, so validating the issuer alone buys you nothing. The condition is the part doing the work.

Note what it matches on. 

assertion.repository
would also work here, but it matches a name and names get renamed, or claimed by someone else once you release them. 
repository_id
and 
repository_owner_id
are immutable, which is why Google recommends mapping those instead.

Give the exploit somewhere safe to run

Verification runs attack code that nobody reviewed, written on demand, pointed at a mock target, doing what the vulnerability class implies. As recent headlines have reminded everyone, the last thing you want is an autonomous agent deciding the fastest way to complete a task is to break out of its container and port-scan your internal network.

Before you can trust the verdict, you have to answer two important questions: Where does that code execute, and what can it reach while it does? The answer is to run it as a Cloud Run job.

Every Cloud Run instance is sandboxed, and jobs always run in the second-generation execution environment, a microVM with full Linux compatibility. The execution starts, does one thing, and exits.

Figure 5: The exploit runs in an instance that holds nothing and lives for one finding. Only the verdict leaves.

Then empty the room. Give the job a service account of its own and grant it nothing beyond the API that writes the exploit. It needs no registry access, because Cloud Run imports the container image when you deploy rather than pulling it at the instance start.

Skip the Compute Engine default account, which may carry 

roles/editor
depending on your organization policy. Take the network away too: Direct VPC egress into a subnet with no route out means code that can't call anywhere can't exfiltrate what it finds or fetch a second stage. 

Run one job per finding. The execution ends, the instance goes with it, and the verdict is the only thing that outlives either.

Cloud Run sandboxes or agent sandboxes close the last gap. In the instance, process execution is isolated from the parent workload, its environment variables, its secrets, and the Google Cloud metadata server, so the credential the platform hands out by default is out of reach as well. It's built for agents running code they just wrote.

Get started today

You can build an autonomous GitOps security agent today. Start with the reference implementation at codemender-gitops.

entries.content:
Bei Li

Principal Engineer

Deepak Dayama

Group Product Manager

To answer a complex business question, an AI agent must understand two things: what happened, and why. The what is a governed metric, like revenue at risk; the why is the network of relationships that produced it. Because metric definitions, a.k.a. measures, traditionally live in business intelligence (BI) platforms while relationships live in knowledge graphs, an AI agent only ever sees half the picture. It guesses the rest, leading to confident but sometimes wrong answers. To solve this hallucination problem, we introduced measures in BigQuery, which are now generally available.

Historically, organizations needing both BI and knowledge graphs had to run two siloed technology stacks: one to calculate reliable metrics, the other to map out entity relationships. Bridging them entailed brittle data pipelines and runtime reconciliation by analysts and AI agents, who held the connections in their heads or in sprawling prompts. This patchwork approach wasn't just slow and expensive — it’s where data governance broke down, as every analyst and prompt may define joins and metrics differently.

Figure 1: A unified model for defining BI metrics and knowledge graphs in one place, for powering AI agents, SQL, GQL and dashboards.

To replace manual reconciliation, you need a single model that understands both the structure of your business and the math that measures it. BigQuery measures builds directly on BigQuery Graph to deliver that unified foundation. By defining measures directly on the graph entities they describe, your BI dashboards and AI agents don't just get a number they can trust — they get the relational context behind it. Finally, they can reliably answer both the what and the why.

"With BigQuery measures, we can now deliver self-documenting data products. Defining measures natively in BigQuery ensures Looker Dashboards, Conversational Agents and our Data team queries operate on identical logic, guaranteeing metric alignment across leadership and significantly reducing data team maintenance overhead." - Amanda Reelick, Head of Data Enablement, Woolworths NZ

One model to answer both the what and the why

Let's walk through an example. Suppose your retail bank's risk analytics team spots a sudden spike in transaction activity in the Prague district. You need to know whether this represents healthy customer growth or concentrated risk exposure. Answering requires two pieces of evidence: how much money actually moved (the what), and which specific accounts it flowed through (the why). At most banks, getting that answer takes two teams, two tools, and two numbers that are rarely reconciled.

With BigQuery, your underlying data is already in place — whether in native tables or in a borderless Lakehouse. With a single schema, you can define a semantic model directly over your existing transaction, account, and district tables — with no data movement and no secondary system:

To determine whether the Prague spike reflects broad growth or concentrated exposure, your team checks whether the transaction volume is spread across many accounts or driven by just a few. Using 

GRAPH_EXPAND
, you flatten the graph and roll up both measures with the 
AGG()
function:

You can ensure accurate reporting by using measures that have been “grain-locked” — where a fixed level of granularity has been assigned to how facts and dimensions are modeled. Because a single account can have thousands of transactions, joining the two tables can duplicate account rows. A standard SQL 

COUNT(account_id)
would overcount those accounts, leaving your risk and finance teams with conflicting numbers. BigQuery measures preserve the native grain of each entity, counting every account only once regardless of how the tables are joined.

The second half of the investigation is about connectivity: Which accounts are driving the Prague activity? You can answer that with a traversal in GQL (the ISO-standard Graph Query Language) over the exact same model:

Neither query requires a separate system, and both evaluate against the same governed definitions.

New features in BigQuery measures

While the preview introduced grain-locked measures tightly integrated with BigQuery Graph, real-world production analytics demand more than basic sums — and enterprise AI agents need programmatic ways to discover and interpret those metrics. The GA of BigQuery measures focuses on two key areas: richer modeling and visualization for complex business logic, and native semantic discovery for the agentic ecosystem.

Richer modeling, querying and BI visualization

To enable more expressive and flexible measure definitions, 

MEASURE()
supports both composite expressions and derived measures; this capability is GA. Rather than repeating conditional logic across queries, you can define baseline aggregates once and compose them into higher-order calculations on the same table using 
AGG()
. BigQuery validates these formula dependencies at schema compilation time to catch circular references or invalid aggregations early. Downstream dashboards and AI agents can then query complex ratios and net metrics at any dimensionality with consistent accuracy.

For example, on your 

Trans
node, you can define settled volume alongside total volume, and then derive unsettled volume and unsettled percentage directly from those building blocks:

Query across multiple fact tables

Enterprise data models routinely span multiple business processes. Joining separate fact tables that share a common dimension — such as transactions and credit cards linked to the same bank account — traditionally causes a "chasm trap," where cross-fact multiplication inflates both metrics.

The new 

start_node
argument in 
GRAPH_EXPAND
solves this by isolating each fact table into its own expansion tree. BigQuery evaluates each measure at its native grain before joining the results on the shared entity:

By expanding each fact table from its own root (

Trans
and 
Card
), each branch maintains its exact grain — even for accounts with transactions but no issued cards.

Visualize in Data Studio

With the updated BigQuery connector in Data Studio, you can now connect directly to BigQuery graphs and build interactive visualizations powered by native measures. Data Studio honors the aggregation logic defined in your graph model, keeping complex calculations consistent across charts while preventing accidental client-side re-aggregations.

Built for the agentic era

Attach business meaning to your measures

In a large enterprise schema, it’s nice to be able to attach business meaning to your measures, as multiple metrics often share similar names. In our banking model alone, 

total_trans_amount
, 
settled_volume
, and 
unsettled_volume
could all casually be called "volume" by a business user. That ambiguity can trip up both analysts building reports and AI agents translating natural-language prompts into SQL.

With the GA, you can embed rich semantic metadata directly into each measure definition using the 

OPTIONS
clause, including plain-language description strings, domain synonyms, and custom key-value extensions:

Because this business context lives inside the schema alongside the SQL formula, your semantic definitions travel wherever the metric is queried.

Make measures discoverable to humans and AI agents

BigQuery directly integrates with Knowledge Catalog to create a unified discovery and consumption loop for both people and machines:

  • Enterprise-wide context discovery in Knowledge Catalog: BigQuery Graph and measures metadata is automatically ingested and searchable in Knowledge Catalog as a native resource alongside tables, views, and routines. Data stewards, analysts, and AI agents can search across the catalog using business synonyms or descriptions, inspect governance tags, and view the underlying measure’s SQL definitions (such as 

    SUM(CASE WHEN is_settled = TRUE...)
    ) to verify how each metric is calculated before using it. In Knowledge Catalog, you can also enrich graph metadata with business glossaries and stewardship context, uniting asset discovery, business meaning, and mathematical measures in a single pane so users and agents can work from the same context.

  • Runtime schema introspection in BigQuery: Calling 

    BQ.SHOW_GRAPH_EXPAND_SCHEMA
    returns an expanded graph's schema as JSON without scanning underlying tables, flagging metrics with 
    "is_measure": true
    alongside their descriptions and synonyms. Passing 
    flatten_results => FALSE
    preserves your entity hierarchy as nested  
    ROW
    (
    STRUCT
    ) types, letting agents inspect the relational tree and query paths like 
    Account.District.city
    directly.

Connect across your data and AI ecosystem

Finally, BigQuery measures integrates across the Google Cloud data and AI stack so you can author, reuse, and query semantics in the tools you already use:

  • Author with AI: Use the graph skills in Data Agent Kit to scaffold, author, and validate BigQuery measure definitions using natural-language prompts in your preferred AI coding environment.

  • Reuse existing LookML models: If you already model business metrics in Looker, you can model once using LookML-based derived analytic models to compile Explores, joins, and measures directly into native BigQuery Graph models.

  • Query with natural language: Unified graph and measure definitions are supported out-of-the-box in Conversational Analytics, enabling business users and AI agents to ask complex questions against governed metrics in plain natural language.

Get started with BigQuery measures

The primary advantage of this unified model is that you can build from the foundation you already have. If you already run a BI semantic layer, take a governed metric and define it directly on the entity it describes; if your foundation is a knowledge graph, attach a unified measure to your most frequent traversal. Whichever side you start from, you are building a single source of truth for both your BI dashboards and your AI agents.

To see unified semantics in action, watch the BigQuery measures introduction video, or dive into the BigQuery measures documentation and BigQuery Graph overview. When you are ready to build hands-on, try our step-by-step codelabs for music streaming analytics.

entries.summary: Standard Network Policies limit you to applying policies at the namespace level, but ClusterNetworkPolicy (CNP) lets you apply granular networking policies across an entire cluster. In this post, we'll explore u
entries.content:
Ammett Williams

Developer Relations Engineer

Standard Network Policies limit you to applying policies at the namespace level, but ClusterNetworkPolicy (CNP) lets you apply granular networking policies across an entire cluster. When you use CNP, you can easily scale security and governance policies. Recently, I experimented with this functionality in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and saw the benefits for myself.

In this post, we'll explore using CNP to control traffic to an LLM and cluster. If you want to jump right into a hands-on lab, check out this Codelab: Secure AI Inference Workloads with GKE ClusterNetworkPolicy.

How CNP works

CNP follows a three-tier flow with a precedence match:

  • Admin tier (top precedence): Cluster administrator enforces mandatory security rules that can't be bypassed (for example, blocking metadata access).

  • Network policy tier (middle precedence): Standard namespace-scoped policies that are managed by application teams to control ingress and egress for their microservices.

  • Baseline tier (bottom precedence): Cluster administrator establishes fallback defaults (for example, a default-deny posture across namespaces).

Design pattern example

The aim of the experiment in the Codelab is to restrict traffic to the LLM namespace, allow only authorized clients, and prevent cluster-wide access to the metadata API except for DNS port 53. It uses these services:

  • Virtual Private Cloud (VPC): Provides private networking, subnets for pods and services, and secure outbound egress via Cloud NAT.

  • TPU v5e: High-efficiency accelerator hardware (2x2 topology) running optimized model inference.

  • GKE: Managed Kubernetes platform that's powered by GKE Dataplane V2 (eBPF) to enforce multi-tier networking policies.

  • Gemma 4 (google/gemma-4-E2B-it): Lightweight open model served with vLLM to act as a sensitive AI workload.

  • ClusterNetworkPolicy (CNP): Cluster-wide policies that let administrators enforce mandatory administrator and baseline guardrails across all namespaces.

  • NetworkPolicies: Standard namespace-scoped rules that let developers grant access to authorized clients.

  • Cloud Logging / GKE Network Policy Logging: Captures real-time packet verdicts (

    allow
    /
    deny
    ) and policy audit trails.

Putting it together: Setup overview

Setting up this environment begins with building a custom private network infrastructure and deploying your TPU-enabled clusters:

  • Custom VPC & Cloud NAT: Establish a custom VPC with a dedicated subnet that hosts primary nodes, plus secondary CIDR IP address ranges for GKE pods (

    10.20.0.0/16
    ) and services (
    10.30.0.0/20
    ). A Cloud Router and Cloud NAT are configured to handle secure outbound egress for nodes while blocking inbound internet exposure.

  • GKE Standard cluster: Spin up a Standard GKE cluster running GKE Dataplane V2 (

    ADVANCED_DATAPATH
    ). GKE Dataplane V2 acts as the core engine that leverages eBPF under the hood to enforce both standard and cluster-scoped policies dynamically.

  • Dedicated TPU v5e node pool: Provision a node pool featuring 

    ct5lp-hightpu-4t
    machines arranged in a 2x2 topology slice. The nodes carry a dedicated taint (
    google.com/tpu=present:NoSchedule
    ) to ensure that only accelerator workloads run on them.

  • Deploying the Gemma 4 workload: Isolate the pods by creating three distinct namespaces:

    • gemma-llm
      (
      tier: ai-core
      ): Serves the lightweight Gemma 4 model using the high-performance 
      vllm/vllm-tpu:latest
      engine on port 8000.
    • client-ns
      (
      tier: app-frontend
      ): Runs the authorized chat client that must query the model.
    • untrusted-tenant
      (
      tier: untrusted
      ): Represents an unauthorized probe container simulating a rogue client.

Securing the LLM and metadata: Code walkthrough

By default in Kubernetes, all cross-namespace and egress traffic is open. To enforce a defense-in-depth posture, we apply network policies across the GKE evaluation tiers.

Step 1: Establish zero-trust posture (baseline tier)

To deny all unauthorized ingress cluster-wide, the cluster administrator applies a ClusterNetworkPolicy at the baseline tier. This tier acts as a fallback safety net.

How it works

  • Precedence placement: Setting 

    tier: Baseline
    places this policy at the very bottom of the GKE evaluation chain, and the 
    priority: 1000
    value orders it within that tier. It only processes traffic that hasn't matched a rule in any higher tier.

  • Global target: Specifying 

    subject.namespaces: {}
    ensures that this fallback applies globally to every pod in every namespace.

  • DNS isolation exemption: The first ingress rule accepts incoming DNS traffic on TCP and UDP port 53. Without this explicit exemption, cluster-wide DNS resolution would fail.

  • Fallback deny: The second rule matches any incoming pod-to-pod connection attempt and drops it. At this stage, both the 

    client-ns
    and 
    untrusted-tenant
    namespaces are blocked from contacting Gemma.

Step 2: Delegate access to developers (networkpolicy tier)

With the baseline default-deny active, the application team that manages 

gemma-llm
can safely delegate access to legitimate clients. They define a standard namespace-scoped 
NetworkPolicy
to allow incoming port 8000 traffic from 
rag-agent
 pods in the 
client-ns
namespace.

How it works

  • Developer control: This resource resides within the 

    gemma-llm
    namespace and it's managed directly by the developer, matching the GKE focus on operational separation.

  • Middle precedence matching: Standard Kubernetes 

    NetworkPolicies
    map directly to the NetworkPolicy Tier. Because this tier is evaluated before the baseline tier, incoming TCP packets from the authorized client to port 8000 match this rule and are immediately accepted.

  • Fall-through block: Connections that originate from the 

    untrusted-tenant
    namespace fail to match this rule, pass through to the baseline tier, and are dropped.

Step 3: Enforce global egress guardrails (admin tier)

By default, Pods can query the GKE link-local Compute Engine metadata server (

169.254.169.254
). Those queries expose instance metadata and potentially high-privilege service account tokens. To lock this down, the cluster administrator applies an egress guardrail at the highest tier in the GKE hierarchy.

How it works

  • Admin tier precedence: Deploying this policy in the admin tier ensures that it's evaluated first, and priority 10 orders it within that tier. GKE processes this policy before standard NetworkPolicies and baseline rules.

  • Controlled delegation: The 

    delegate-all-ingress
    and 
    delegate-other-egress
    rules have an 
    action: Pass
    directive that instructs the engine to forward evaluation down to the next tier for remaining in-cluster traffic.

  • Inviolable guardrail: When any pod attempts to query 

    169.254.169.254/32
    on non-DNS ports, the query matches the 
    block-metadata-server-global
    rule and it's dropped. Because this drop occurs at the top admin tier, it can't be bypassed or overridden, even if a namespace developer deploys an allow-all egress policy.

Verifying with Observability for GKE

Verifying and auditing security policies is straightforward using the built-in telemetry capabilities of GKE Dataplane V2:

  • Hubble eBPF streams: Provides real-time, kernel-level packet inspection without injecting sidecars. Administrators can stream live network flows to observe policy verdicts as they happen, making it easy to validate allowed communication paths and identify dropped packets immediately.

  • GKE Network Logging and Cloud Logging: Automatically exports structured connection telemetry and policy enforcement verdicts directly into Cloud Logging. Teams can filter and alert on policy decisions using attributes such as 

    disposition="deny"
    , source/destination namespaces, and 
    jsonPayload.policies[0].name
    to maintain audit compliance and investigate blocked connection attempts.

CNP can be useful and, as always, when you use it in your production environment, you'll need to plan and design the rules based on your setup.

Next steps

Take a deeper dive and find more information on these features:

  • ClusterNetworkPolicy in GKE: Balancing control and autonomy for your microservices

  • Configuring GKE ClusterNetworkPolicy

Want to ask a question, find out more, or share a thought? Connect with me on LinkedIn!
